nodes.label: Mutual TLS on the cluster transport
nodes.rationale: The transport defaults to plain TCP without authentication, which is fine on a private network and not fine across an untrusted boundary; mTLS addresses eavesdropping and unauthorized joins together, because with a shared CA every connection needs a peer cert in both directions.

nodes.label: TcpTransport TLS options
nodes.rationale: cert and key carry the material itself, not a path — nothing in the transport reads from disk and no runtime accepts a filename. requestClientCert defaults to true whenever ca is present, since a trust bundle on a cluster listener has no other purpose.

nodes.label: The certificate also decides which node
nodes.rationale: mTLS answered may-this-peer-be-in-the-cluster but never is-this-peer-who-it-claims: the hello frame carries an address and no credential, so one CA-signed node could announce itself under another member address — and every gossip-authority rule keys off the connection peer, so they are exactly as strong as the identity underneath them.

nodes.label: What a shared certificate cannot do
nodes.rationale: Two nodes presenting the same host certificate are indistinguishable to the check and no certificate-based rule could separate them; issue per-node certificates naming systemName@host if you need node-level identity.

nodes.label: Three configurations refused at bind time
nodes.rationale: An incomplete server credential used to be a silent downgrade: the listener bound plaintext while the same options still dialled out over TLS, so the cluster formed and the node looked TLS-configured — a half-applied secret rotation was enough. It now throws, which means a node quietly serving plaintext fails to start rather than coming up mis-secured.

nodes.label: Deno cannot host an mTLS listener
nodes.rationale: Deno.listenTls takes only a cert and a key with no way to request or verify a client certificate, so the listener would authenticate nobody; a Deno node can still join, so in a mixed deployment keep the seed nodes on Node.js or Bun.

nodes.label: Cluster transport threat model
nodes.rationale: Eavesdropping, MITM, unauthorized join, stolen certs, hostile frames, decode amplification, half-open and silent sockets, unbounded registries, pre-claimed addresses, replayed gossip and spoofed discovery — each with its stated mitigation.

nodes.label: Firewall the cluster port
nodes.rationale: Even with TLS and auth, expose 2552 narrowly: pods talk to pods, nothing goes through a Service, Ingress or LoadBalancer.

nodes.label: Pinning what the resolver may say
nodes.rationale: A seed answer arrives before any certificate has been checked. It cannot let an attacker join where certificates bind the claimed address — but that guarantee is configuration-dependent, so pinnedAddresses is defence in depth and the only discovery-layer control left standing when mTLS is not in place.

nodes.label: What the wire edge rejects
nodes.rationale: Frames used to be cast rather than checked, so null alone was an eight-byte remote process kill needing no handshake. Two tiers deliberately: a frame failing validation is dropped and the connection stays up, because one bad frame should not cost a healthy peer its link, while a handler that throws drops the connection because that is the case nobody understands.

nodes.label: Linear decode buffer
nodes.rationale: The peer chooses the chunk split, and the decoder used to rebuild its accumulator per chunk, so one frame cost work quadratic in the chunk count — a 16 MiB frame in TCP-sized writes is ~12 000 chunks and about 100 GB of copying, roughly 6000x amplification on bytes never sent, reachable before the hello gate. Doubling growth makes it 1x.

nodes.label: Stall and handshake deadlines
nodes.rationale: An incomplete frame may sit 30 s without another byte, re-armed on every chunk so a slow link is never punished, only silence. The handshake gets 5 s from accept — the case an incomplete frame cannot cover, since a socket sending no bytes is not stalled mid-frame — and the deadline is gone once hello lands, because an established peer between gossip rounds is idle by design.

nodes.label: Inbound connection cap of 1024
nodes.rationale: Far above any realistic fully-meshed topology; what it removes is multiplying per-connection cost by opening sockets in a loop. The newest connection is refused rather than an established one evicted, because eviction would let an attacker push real peers off the node — and the cap is only worth what its slot turnover is worth, which is why the handshake deadline is its pair.

nodes.label: Per-registry caps on well-formed frames
nodes.rationale: Shape validation says a frame is readable, not that acting on it is free: a peer naming 100 000 topics sent one perfectly legal frame and the receiver allocated 100 000 entries. A claim over a cap is dropped and logged rather than refused on the wire, while a local Subscribe over a cap is answered with SubscribeRejected, because the caller can do something about it.

nodes.label: Why membership needs two caps
nodes.rationale: A phantom live member is watched by the failure detector and dropped seconds after the attacker stops feeding it; a record gossiped as removed is watched by nothing until the tombstone TTL a day later, so the tombstone flood is the one that persists. Both caps are charged on the bucket a record moves into, because charging only entry creation let the two caps trade headroom and grow the map without bound while respecting both at every step.

nodes.label: Who may say what
nodes.rationale: Merges used to be decided purely by version magnitude, and versions are seeded from Date.now(), so an attacker could always pick a winning number. Nobody downgrades us, and a third-party claim needs a sender with standing — both keyed on the connection peer rather than the payload from field, since that field is the one thing an attacker fully controls. Unreachability is deliberately exempt, because it is inherently a third-party observation.

nodes.label: A sharding directive needs the coordinator behind it
nodes.rationale: A region used to treat any sharding.* frame as a framework directive, so one small frame from anyone past hello could hand off shards or publish an allocation map. It now claims its own path on the envelope router, which supplies the connection peer, and wraps the frame in a class instance a JSON body cannot mint — both halves load-bearing, since a non-canonical path misses the handler lookup and an authenticated peer is any member.

nodes.label: A region can only speak for its own node
nodes.rationale: Every message a coordinator accepts is a claim about the sender own node, and its only gate was isLeader(), which answers am-I-authoritative and never may-this-sender-speak-for-that-region. One forged Register seized every shard of a type and one RegionTerminated evicted a region without a HandOff, leaving two owners for one live shard and two writers on one persistenceId — one forgery, every subsequent hop authentic.

nodes.label: maxVersionSkewMs, the version-claim budget
nodes.rationale: Highest-version-wins also decided the first mention of an address, so a stranger could claim the address the next pod is about to get, with roles that drive routing, sharding, singleton hosting and downing quorums. The budget applies to every merge, because the narrower first-sighting rule could be stepped around by introducing the address first, and any rule letting a record earn the wider budget fails the same way one step later.

nodes.label: Per-sender gossip frame sequence
nodes.rationale: A captured frame stays valid indefinitely, and against a deleted entry the first-sighting branch has no lower version bound at all, so replaying a downed member pre-down record brought it back with its roles. A sequence must also be plausible: merging an implausible one but refusing to adopt it let a captured frame with one field rewritten be merged again on every delivery, without limit.

nodes.label: Address incarnation, carried but not yet acted on
nodes.rationale: The field is optional on the wire so either version understands the other — and an optional field is bypassed by stripping it, so a refusal keyed on a mismatch is one an attacker opts out of while a legitimate older peer walks into it. Requiring it breaks all eight address-bearing fields at once and waits on wire-protocol versioning. Three residual gaps stay open for exactly that reason.

nodes.label: These rules are not authentication
nodes.rationale: They remove the free-for-all — a claim now needs standing this node granted rather than a large number — but on a cluster with no peer certificates an attacker can announce itself, wait to be promoted and then satisfy the second rule. Under mTLS the claimed address must match the certificate, which is what gives the rules a real subject.
